1:
Gill treats the words as a continuation, the same law of the trespass offering being still in hand and only the persons concerned changing. Keil looks ahead: what follows was addressed to Aaron and his sons, the priests, and sets out the duties that fell to them and the rights that pertained to them in the sacrifices — much of it repeated from the general regulations, but most of it new and of real importance to the institution of sacrifice. Ellicott uses the opening to correct a claim repeated in good commentaries, that these verses belong to the previous chapter in the Hebrew and that the English translators unfortunately took the division from the Septuagint. Nothing, he says, could be more erroneous. The Hebrew manuscripts have no division into chapters at all; the text is cut instead into sections, of which the Pentateuch has six hundred and sixty-nine and Leviticus alone ninety-eight against the twenty-seven chapters of our version. The chapter divisions now printed in Hebrew Bibles were taken from the Christians in the fourteenth century for controversial purposes, and the verse figures are later still.

Henry notices first what the offences have in common. Every instance concerns a neighbour, yet the whole is called a trespass against the Lord, because an injury done to a man is an affront offered to his Maker — he that speaks evil of his brother speaks evil of the law, and so of the Law-maker; and however mean the person wronged, the wrong reflects upon the God who made the command of loving our neighbour second only to that of loving himself. He counts five kinds. Denying a trust, when a man claims as his own what was only lent him or left in his keeping — property and truth must be maintained for the benefit of human society. Defrauding a partner, by claiming sole interest where the interest is joint. Disowning a manifest wrong, when a man has the front to lie about a thing taken by violence, which ordinarily cannot be hid. Deceiving in commerce, by withholding what is due or extorting what is not. And detaining what is found: a man must not call it his own at once but seek out the owner, which is doing as he would be done by, and if he backs his denial with a false oath he affronts the God who witnesses all speech and in an oath is himself appealed to.

On the remedy Henry puts the order plainly: satisfaction to the brother comes first, and the wrong must be restored with its fifth part added, to cover loss and trouble both. Till restitution is made to the utmost of our power we cannot have the comfort of forgiveness, for keeping what was unjustly got avows the taking, and the two together make one continued act of unrighteousness — to repent is to undo what we have done amiss, which we cannot be said to do till we restore, as Zaccheus did. The offering itself could make no satisfaction, but signified the atonement Christ was to make when he made his soul a trespass offering, the same word standing in Isaiah. Calvin marks what is new here, that Moses has left the expiation of oversights and now prescribes reconciliation for sin committed wilfully and by design. That must not be turned into licence, since it is a blasphemous insult to God to take occasion for sin from his readiness to pardon; but neither may we make him inexorable to voluntary sin, which would overthrow the hope of salvation in the holiest men. Novatus troubled the ancient Church with that severity, and its rigid censors, Calvin thinks, are the grossest hypocrites — which of them on honest examination would find himself free of concupiscence? God is not changed, nor is our condition worse than the fathers', who had sacrifices appointed for voluntary offences.
2:
Why an injury to a man is called a trespass against the Lord the three answer alike. Gill grants that all sin is against him, but marks these as more apparently so, being contrary not only to his will but to the good of society — and worst where he is sworn by and appealed to as a witness in a case at once injurious and false. Ellicott puts it that the trespass against God is strictly a violation of a neighbour's property, and that since fraud and plunder are the most subversive of social life, such a crime is described as an insult to the founder and sovereign ruler of the people. Wesley gives three reasons: the offence violates a society of which God is author, president and defender; it is a secret sin, of which he alone is witness and judge; and his name is abused in it by perjury.

Ellicott explains the custom the first case rests on. To leave valuables with a neighbour was, and still is, common in the East, where there are no establishments for keeping private treasure; a man going a journey would otherwise hide his things underground and risk forgetting the spot — which is why the Hebrew word for treasure means what is hidden, and why Scripture speaks of hidden riches of secret places and of searching as for hid treasure. From that practice, he adds, the apostle takes his confidence that God is able to keep what has been committed to him. Wesley reads the second clause as trade rather than trust, one man putting something into another's hand not to keep but to improve for the common benefit, and thinks the phrase comes from the joining of hands that confirmed such bargains; the violence of the third clause he takes as done secretly, since the whole passage concerns sins that no witness could prove. Clarke draws the same conclusion from the evidence: property was often delivered without witnesses, so the holder might deny receiving it and the depositor prove nothing, while a man might equally accuse his neighbour of keeping what was never entrusted — and because the truth was often past finding out without a revelation, the penalties are kept moderate.

On the lost property Gill has the finder call it his own at once and never inquire after the owner, and reports the reason Maimonides gives for restoring it, that besides being a virtue in itself the practice has a reciprocal usefulness, since a man who will not restore another's losings will not have his own restored. Clarke is harder, and cites the Roman lawyers, who counted a finder who converted goods to his own use a thief whether he knew the owner or not, ignorance doing nothing to lessen the theft; he adds that the Dyrbaeans between Bactria and India would not touch lost property even on the public road, that in Alfred's England golden bracelets hung untouched on the highways, and that one of Solon's laws was, take not up what you laid not down — though when due inquiry has been made and no owner appears, the finder may keep it. Ellicott refers the false swearing to all five cases, and explains why the fine is lighter here than the fourfold restitution of Exodus: that law deals with a man convicted in court by witnesses, this with one whom nothing could have convicted, confessing of his own compunction — which is what makes it a case for a trespass offering. Both he and Wesley press the timing, that restitution belongs to the day of confession and must not be delayed. Calvin takes the priest's part for the whole point: the victim was never itself the price of redemption, expiation being founded on the priesthood, so the offering is passive rather than active as regards the man, who brings nothing of his own but receives.
8:
Gill and Clarke think the book breaks here, not seven verses earlier. Gill supposes a pause here, and notes that a new section begins at this point in the Hebrew copies; Clarke goes further, that the Jews open the twenty-fifth section of the law here and that the sixth chapter undoubtedly should commence with it, what precedes belonging to the fifth — the best Hebrew Bibles, he says, begin the chapter here. Ellicott counts it the fourth use of the formula and marks the turn: hitherto the law had told the people how to bring their oblations, and now the priests are told how to conduct the service. Henry draws a lesson from that turn. The priests were rulers in the house of God, but these rulers must themselves be ruled, and those who had the command of others must themselves be commanded — let ministers remember that not commissions only but commands were given to Aaron and his sons.

How the night burning worked they reconstruct together. Keil observes that the verb is wanting in the first clause and supplied only in the second though it governs both, and that the opening pronoun cannot stand for an imperative, the passages Knobel cites being of a wholly different kind; the instructions apply first to the evening burnt offering, the basis of all the rest. Clarke argues from the practical difficulty: if the whole offering were laid on at once it could not burn all night, so the priests must have sat up by turns and fed the fire until morning, the morning offering being likewise consumed piecemeal through the day; and he thinks the fat was burnt chiefly at night for the light and the convenience of tending the fire. Ellicott would render it that the burnt offering shall lie upon the fire and the fire be fed by it, and notes that in the second Temple the fat began to burn at midnight, keeping the fire alive till day. Wesley explains why only the night needed a law: the daytime had such a succession of sacrifices that the fire could not fail.

On the ashes Henry has the priest clear the altar each morning in his linen, lay them on the east side furthest from the sanctuary, then change and carry them outside the camp to a clean place. God would have even the ashes preserved for the honour of the altar, and some think the care of them typified the burial of our Saviour, whose body was laid in a garden in a new sepulchre; God would also have the priests do it themselves, to teach that his servants must think nothing beneath them but sin. Of the fire he says that those who keep good houses never let the kitchen fire go out, and that the first came down from heaven, so that while it was kept up every later sacrifice might be reckoned consumed by that fire in token of acceptance — let it once go out and they could not expect it kindled so again, and the Jews say it never did until the captivity. Calvin explains why the details are pressed so far: God prefers obedience to sacrifice and would leave nothing doubtful in the rites, the purity of holy things being corrupted by the smallest human invention. The perpetuity had the same end, that the offerings should always burn with heavenly fire, God having kindled it miraculously at Aaron's consecration, at Solomon's temple and at Elijah's sacrifice, and thereafter using men's hands while the origin remained his. He knows that Persia had a perpetual fire and Rome its Vestal guardians, and suspects a foolish mimicry — the devil imitating God as an ape imitates a man — but holds the ban on strange fire to be simply a ban on men adding anything of their own to the doctrine of the Law.
10:
Gill explains the name of the linen garment, that the word means his measure, a robe cut exactly to the body and reaching to the feet — an emblem, he adds, of the purity of Christ our high priest, who being without sin could take away the sin of others by offering himself without spot. Ellicott counts the sacerdotal dress at four pieces: the tunic, a close robe of fine linen reaching to the feet; the drawers, which in the second Temple reached the knee; a girdle three fingers wide and thirty-two cubits long; and a turban fastened with ribbons. Only two are named here, but he thinks all four meant, the rest passed over for brevity or covered by the first word, which is why some versions put it in the plural. On the ashes he would render the clause as those into which the fire had consumed the offering, and reports that a priest was chosen by lot to lift a shovelful each morning; Wesley notes only that the ashes are the wood burnt down.

The change of dress they explain alike and value differently. Clarke has the priests approach the altar in their holiest garments and put on others to carry out the ashes, the holy dress serving only in the holy place, and defines the clean place as one where no carcass or filth was laid, the ashes being holy as remains of offerings made by fire. Ellicott guards the other side: the second set, though less holy, was not common either, since removing the ashes was still a priestly act, the sacred robes being laid up meanwhile in cells within the precincts. He adds what care was taken at the far end — the place sheltered against the wind, the ashes laid down gently rather than flung, and no stranger allowed to gather them or make profit of them. Wesley puts it simply, that the second garments served because this was no sacred but a common work.

Gill sets out three fires kept on the altar: a large pile for the daily sacrifice, a smaller called the pile of the incense, from which fire was carried in a censer for the morning and evening incense, and a third kept only to preserve the flame, which on Maimonides' judgment is the one meant here; R. Joses places the great pile eastward, the second south-west nearer the ascent, and the third wherever seemed fit. Ellicott describes the same three in the second Temple and traces the history: the fire burned unquenched until Nebuchadnezzar destroyed the house, and the priests carried captive into Persia are said to have hid it in a pit, whence it was restored in Nehemiah's time — though the authorities of our Lord's day reckon it among the five things wanting in the second Temple. He reads the repeated clause as a caution to the priest clearing the ashes, not to knock the fat pieces which feed the flame off the altar with them. Keil states the purpose exactly: the fire was kept up not to preserve the heavenly flame but so that the burnt offering itself should never cease, being the appointed sign of an uninterrupted worship the covenant nation could not suspend without unfaithfulness — and for the same reason, he notes, other nations kept fire always burning on the altars of their chief gods. Clarke instances the Persian Magi and the Parsees after them, who keep it still by command of the Zend Avesta, and the Sagnika Brahmin, who preserves the fire kindled at his investiture, uses it at his wedding and every burnt offering, and is burnt with it at the last. Wesley gives the reason from the Israelite side: a fire once come down from heaven was preserved partly to leave no temptation to offer strange fire, partly to teach them whence the acceptance of every sacrifice came.
14:
Gill notes that the rules were given before and are repeated with additions, and Keil says which is which: the first two verses repeat the earlier chapter, the new matter beginning with what was left unburnt — the priests were to bake it without leaven and eat it in the court of the tabernacle, as their share of the firings of Jehovah, most holy like the sin and trespass offerings, and eaten only by the males of their families, a statute for ever. Ellicott adds two points: the sons of Aaron, though the words are literal, take in the lineal descendants who succeeded to the office, they and no layman being allowed to offer; and before the altar means its fore part, the south-easterly corner. Wesley distinguishes the case in hand from the priest's own offering, this being brought alone and by any of the people, since a priest's must have been wholly burnt.

Henry weighs their portion against their labour. The burnt offerings laid much work on them for little profit, the flesh being wholly burnt and only the skin left; here they are made amends, a handful going to the altar and the rest being their own. It is God's will that his ministers be provided for, and what is given them he accepts as offered to himself; and since all Christians are spiritual priests, they too share in the sacrifices they offer, for it is not God who gains by them. Let God have the frankincense, he says, and the priests the flour and oil: what we give him the glory of we may take to ourselves the comfort of. Ellicott states the principle, that those who minister at the altar should live of the altar, which is why they had no inheritance in the land. Clarke supplies the measures — an omer of flour, a tenth of an ephah, was the least even the poorest might bring, commonly with a log of oil, something over half a pint; more might be offered, but no less. Gill observes that no quantity is prescribed, which he takes as leaving it to the offerer, the gift being freewill.

Three conditions govern the eating. It must be unleavened, what was offered to God having no leaven in it and the priests having it as the altar had it — thus, Henry adds, must we keep the feast with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth; Gill reads the rule typically, of Christ's sincerity and the uprightness required in the offerer. Ellicott corrects the rendering: it should be unleavened shall it be eaten, the remainder being made into cakes, whereas the inserted with of our version makes the priests eat the offering alongside unleavened bread. It must be eaten in the court, and Henry counts it a crime to carry any out, the eating being itself a sacred rite to be done with reverence; Calvin adds that to leaven meal already dedicated would turn it into common food, a profanation, and that God admits the priests to his own table in a way that raises their office while his presence restrains intemperance and teaches the sobriety due from his servants. And the males only must eat it: of the less holy things, Henry says, the firstfruits and tithes and the breast and shoulder of the peace offerings, the daughters might eat, those being carriageable out of the court, but this was of the most holy. On the closing clause he reports two readings: that every one who touches them shall be holy — holy things for holy persons — or that every thing touching them becomes holy, so that the vessels used must never afterwards serve common uses. Calvin prefers the first: elsewhere the altar and its vessels sanctify what is laid on them, but here laymen are forbidden to touch what is sacred, and the future stands for an imperative.
19:
Ellicott takes the new formula as introducing the oblation of initiation, which follows naturally on the instructions just given. Who exactly brought it is less settled. Gill refers the words to such of Aaron's sons as succeeded him, citing Aben Ezra for him or one of his sons in his room, but reports that some make the common priests bring it too at their initiation, though neither anointed nor bound to continue it daily. Ellicott holds both, on the practice of the second Temple: an ordinary priest brought it once, at his consecration, while the pontiff repeated it daily after the regular holocaust and before the drink offering — and it is to that daily burden, he says, that the apostle alludes in describing a high priest who need not offer first for his own sins. Wesley narrows it to the high priest, the only one anointed in later ages, and notes that the law of his consecration was given before and is repeated for the additions made to it. Clarke reads the day of anointing as a beginning, the statute running from it for ever; Ellicott glosses the phrase as when the ceremony was complete and he entered on his charge, which was the eighth day.

On the making Ellicott corrects three renderings: the measure is a tenth of an ephah, an omer, halved between morning and evening; the pan is better a flat plate; and bringing it baken is rather bringing it well soaked, saturated with oil. The baken pieces mean small roasted cakes, the flour soaked in the pan then divided and baked, apparently to answer the limbs into which a burnt sacrifice was parted. He describes the later practice: the pontiff brought the whole tenth of flour each morning, sanctified it, halved it by the measure kept in the sanctuary, mingled three logs of oil with it, kneaded six cakes from each half, baked them a little and fried them with some of the oil, taking care they stood between baked and raw; then he parted the six into twelve, the number of the shewbread, and brought six at dawn and six at dusk. Gill describes the vessel, a plane and extended plate without covering or hollow or lip, the dough on it made stiff enough not to run off, and mentions the temple chamber where these cakes were prepared. Wesley notes only that the second person addresses the man so anointed and consecrated.

Why none of it might be eaten they answer four ways. Ellicott makes it decency: unlike the laity's mincha, of which all but a handful fell to the minister, this the pontiff presented himself, and it would be unseemly to give a thing to God and eat it too — nor might a lesser priest touch it, being of lower rank than the man who offered. Gill draws the consequence for whoever assisted: he got nothing by it and served the high priest gratis. Clarke states the principle more broadly, that whatever a priest gave was wholly the Lord's and so entirely consumed, since the people's sacrifices fed those who ministered at the altar, whereas had they lived on their own it would have been as if they gave nothing, taking back what they seemed to render. He reports Theodoret's reason, that the rule marked the perfection God required in the ministers of his sanctuary; but prefers Ainsworth's, that the people's gift was eaten by those who made atonement for them, and since no priest, being himself a sinner, could atone for himself, his own might not be eaten but must be wholly burnt — to teach him to look for salvation not by legal service but by Christ, the eating of a sin offering figuring the bearing of the sinner's iniquity. Ellicott adds that the rule was not peculiar to the high priest but covered every meat offering a priest brought.
24:
Ellicott marks the formula as opening not a new law so much as a fuller one, giving closer directions about the laity's sin offering; Gill says the same, rules being added to what went before. On the place of slaughter Clarke and Ellicott agree on the north side, and Ellicott adds that most holy assigns it to a class of sacrifices. Henry sees a figure in the ground itself, some thinking the north side typified the crucifying of Christ on Calvary, north of Jerusalem. Calvin is struck that the two offerings share a place at all. God took care that his people be left in no doubt, true religion being marked off from human imagining by this, that he himself prescribes what is to be done; and since the two differ, it would have been natural to kill them apart, had the mistake not been forestalled by assigning both one place — from which we learn that a single law suffices for worship, if men will not be wise in their own conceits. Yet he will not pretend to more than he has: Moses begins here to distinguish two Hebrew words he had used indifferently, and what the difference was Calvin says plainly he does not know, having seen the guesses of others and nothing certain.

The officiating priest's eating they take for the heart of the rite. Henry has him eat with his sons or other priests, after blood and fat had gone to God, and so bear the iniquity of the congregation. Gill reads it as the sign that he bore the sin of the man who brought the offering, a type of Christ bearing his people's sins on the tree. Ellicott would render it the priest that expiateth sin by it, and explains that the flesh was food and part of their livelihood, the officiating priest being free to invite other priests and their sons as well as his household. Both note the abuse: Clarke that improper persons pressed into the office to secure a secular living, a horrible profanity, and Ellicott that covetous priests are reproached for it by the prophet. Wesley draws the boundary: the rule covers offerings for the sins of rulers or people but not of priests, whose blood went into the tabernacle and whose flesh therefore might not be eaten.

The holiness of the flesh spreads to what it touches. Gill allows none but sacred persons to touch or eat it, and holds the very dishes and knives reserved from common service, to keep up veneration for the sacrifice and for the one it typified. Ellicott prefers the personal rendering, every one that toucheth the flesh, as earlier in the chapter, and describes what followed a splash of blood: a stain on the garment of priest or offerer was washed in the room appointed within the court, where a well supplied the sanctuary, so the blood should not be profaned outside the holy place — and the washing was the priest's office, not the layman's. Henry reads the rule devotionally: such care teaches the regard we owe the blood of Christ, not to be counted common, and to be sprinkled on the conscience rather than the raiment. The broken vessel he takes for an admission of weakness: an earthen pot must be shattered and a brazen one scoured, the defilement clinging to the offering rather than being carried off — whereas the blood of Christ cleanses thoroughly, and after it no cleansing is needed. Keil, whose note on the vessels stands here rather than at the verse prescribing them, gives the reason for both breaking and scouring: no part of the most holy flesh must be left clinging to a pot and desecrated when it is next used. Clarke ends with Ainsworth: since the offering figured him made sin for us, the washing and breaking teach a holy use of that mystery.
28:
Why the earthen pot must be shattered they explain alike. Gill has it porous, so the liquor in which the offering was boiled might soak in and the smell be retained; and since such vessels cost little they were ordered broken. Where the pieces went the Jewish writers could not settle, thinking it indecent that vessels once put to holy uses should lie exposed, and unseemly that heaps of them should gather in the sanctuary — so, Gill says, they framed a miracle, and supposed the ground swallowed them. Ellicott confirms the physical reason: Hebrew earthenware was unglazed, as common ware in the East still is, and would drink up the fat juices, which could not afterwards be washed out; in the second Temple the fragments were buried when they grew many. Brass took no juices, being solid, and adhering flesh came off by washing, the scouring with hot water and the rinsing with cold. Wesley reasons from value as well as substance, that the metal pot was rinsed and not broken because God would not have a thing of worth needlessly wasted, and because a solid substance was less apt to drink in the moisture. Clarke passes on Calmet's restriction, that the rule concerns vessels brought to the court by private men rather than those the priests kept for ordinary service.

Clarke takes the three perpetuals of the chapter together — the meat offering, the fire and the burnt offering — and finds them reflected in the promise that Christ is able to save to the uttermost those who come to God by him, seeing he ever liveth to make intercession. As the meat offering was perpetual, our gratitude for innumerable mercies should be; as the burnt offering was perpetual, the sacrifice of our Lord is to be reckoned a perpetual offering, that men of every age may come to God through one ever living in his sacrificial character, shown even in heaven as the Lamb just slain before the throne; and as the altar fire was never to go out, so the influences of the Spirit in every member of the Church, and the flame of pure devotion in believing hearts, should be permanent and never slack.

Who might share the meal is settled generously. Gill says it was not the single priest who offered but his male children, and those of other priests then on duty; Ellicott adds that he could invite any other priests and their sons, and takes this for the practice behind the apostle's saying that we have an altar whereof they have no right to eat which serve the tabernacle. Keil marks the limit: the flesh was boiled and eaten by the males among the priests alone, and only in the laity's offerings, since those for the high priest and the whole congregation, whose blood went into the tabernacle to complete the expiation, were not eaten but burnt. Gill traces where it was burnt — Ben Gersom puts it in a prepared place east of the court, but a later chapter makes clear it was carried out without the camp. Ellicott would render the last verse but rather than and, and corrects reconciling to making atonement for. Calvin sets the exception in its reason: private men atoned at less expense, only the greater altar in the court being sprinkled, but when the priest reconciled God to the whole people or to himself, that the intercession might be more effectual, he carried blood within the veil — from which the apostle infers, in an apt allusion, that the distinction of meats is abolished, the lesser altar hidden under the Law being now laid open, so that we eat no longer of the legal sacrifices, and since our one Priest has borne his blood into the sanctuary it remains only to go forth with him without the camp.
